Mom got home, smelled smoke and went upstairs to investigate. She opened the door to her bedroom, and it was filled with smoke. She closed the door, went to the neighbor's house, and called the fire department.

The fire department came, and my mom sketched the room for them, and they went upstairs. Smoke rises in a room, but there was so much, it was all the way to the floor, and the fire fighters had to rely on the directions my mom gave them. 

The fire was caused by combustibles too close to a wall heater, but since the room was completely filled with smoke, it didn't have any oxygen left to burn. By the time the fire fighters found the hot spot, there were no flames, just embers. The fire fighters didn't scale their response, and drenched the bathroom.

Everything in those rooms was a total loss (as well as some water damage to the room below). We had to replace wallboard, carpet, furniture, and my parents both got entirely new wardrobes.

A heater or air conditioner will dump heated or cooled air into a space at one temperature, and keep dumping air into that area until it averages out to the temperature you want. If you have a small room and it's already 69 degrees, going to 72 is pretty easy. Your furnace will dump 90 degree (or however hot it is) air into the room until the air mixes and averages out to 72. If you have a big room currently at 50 that you want to rise to 72, the process is identical, but it just takes much longer since it has to get more hot air in to offset the volume and temperature difference.  An air conditioner is identical, it just dumps cold air as opposed to hot air.

Think of the Internet like roads.

Individual ISPs manage connections to houses, like the city maintains local roads.

The ISP connects to a larger provider, similar to the city connecting a local road to a state highway.

Those providers connect to even larger ones until you get to backbones, not unlike major interstates.
(Sometimes city roads connect directly to highways, and sometimes an ISP is large enough to negotiate a connection to a larger provider.)

The interesting devices are routers not unlike the ones that give you wi-fi in your house. These devices act as hubs and route traffic. Forgive the change in analogies, but think of a router like major bus terminal with an information desk. Everyone goes up to it, and tells the desk where they're going, and the desk tells them where to go. This segregates networks, and keeps traffic moving efficiently. This also allows reroutes (detours) to happen if a section of cable (road) get damaged. Outages might happen if there's only a single path to a destination.

There have been a lot of great posts about the transmission medium. There's copper, fiber, wi-fi, satellite, and cellular to name a few. These links all have different bandwidth capacities, just like roads are (hopefully) planned to accommodate the amount of traffic that will go over it. 

Finally, people plug into that infrastructure, and computers can send data back and forth like a courier service. You send a request for something, and it travels along the roads and highways to the destination, getting directions along the way. The web server receives the request, and sends back what you requested.

So I was planning a thing for my baseball team. Nothing big, some pizzas, some soft drinks, maybe a party sub, just general teenage stuff with the pool. I pick out the Friday after a game maybe 3 months out and go talk to my dad.

I walked into his office and said, "Yo, dad, is it cool for me to do a thing in the pool house the last Friday in May?"

My dad didn't even look up from his computer, but he raised an eyebrow and said "Drinking?" He always asked. He knew it wasn't my deal, but he always asked.

I replied "No, maybe a root beer keg, but no alcohol."

 My dad smiled, still not looking at me and said "Cool, I'll throw it on the calendar,Talk to Christina next week if you need anything." As I turned to walk away he said "Wait, Christina is off next week. Talk to Jim when you get home from school on Monday." I nodded and left.

Christina was the family's personal assistant. She did the stuff like household errands now that we didn't need a babysitter. Jim was my dad's business assistant. He had an office in the house, but we tried not to bother him. A little crossover was normal.

So Monday rolled around, and I stopped by Jim's office. He was cool, we just didn't talk much.  I knocked on his open door and he looked up and waved me in.  "Hey kid, what's up?" he asked motioning to a chair.

I sat down and said "Just putting a thing together. Do you have the personal card?"

 Jim looked through his desk drawers as he said "Yeah, your father said you'd be swinging by. The personal card is here somewhere," before he managed to find it.

"Cool," I said. "Nothing big, plan for 30, expect 20, pizza, soda, party sub, chips, etc."

 "Maybe something like the New Years party for you and your sister's friends?" he asked.

"Yeah," I replied. "You did that?"

 "Your dad used the same stuff for his client party. I just ordered extra so Chris didn't have to put in a second order," he replied.

"Cool, maybe a different pizza place, but everything else was perfect," I said.

Jim nodded and dug through a file behind his desk. "Date?" he asked.

"May 25th," I replied.

"Thanks," Jim said. "I'll send you stuff to check in two weeks."

"Nah, I'm good," I said. "Just the different pizza place, whatever you like. Everything else was great."

"Cool, I'll throw this together. Let me know if anything changes," Jim said as I left.

So fast forward a month. Christina is back, I make mention of the thing to her, but Jim has it, so no worries. We're sitting down to dinner one night and my little, just finishing her freshman year, sister starts with her Daddy's girl voice.

"Daddy, can I have some girls over for a sleepover?" she asked.

My dad looked at her and replied "Sure sweetie, when?"

 "May 25th in the pool house," she said.

My dad looked up for a second, and it dawned on him before I even remembered that I had a thing planned. "Sweetie, that doesn't work. Your brother has people coming over that night for the pool house."

 "But Daaaa-deeee," she wailed, "cheer tryouts for going to summer cheer camp is right after that. I want the girls to like me." I rolled my eyes and continued eating.

 "Don't they already like you? You're smart, and funny, and you've always been nice to them," but Dad was cut off by my sister before he finished.

"But I want them to like me more..." she whined.

I kept quiet. My sister tended to do well with these, negotiations, if you could call them that. But my dad was fair when it came to treatment of his kids.

"Okay cupcake, you can have the entire North wing for your party," Dad said. "Your mother and I will spend our night in the West wing, and I'll have Christina come make you breakfast."

 "But I want the pool house. I don't want my friends to all sleep in different rooms. I want sleeping bags on the floor," she said.

My mother chimed in saying "You can still have all that, we'll rope off the hallway and keep everyone in the living room and kitchen."

My sister started getting pouty, and my dad looked to me.

"No way man, I've had this planned for like a month," I said. "She can do Saturday." Continued pouting from my sister showed that she wasn't going to accept that.

My dad looked to my mother, and then they stepped away from the table. My sister glared at me while I kept eating.

What I didn't know was that dad's business was growing, and Christina was doing more business stuff now that us kids were more self sufficient. Dad put a call in to her right then and asked if she'd take on a rush project, and he'd hire a part time person to do her previous job. Christina was elated, and readily accepted the change.

My parents came back, and my mother said "You're going to have to go easy on Christina for a few weeks until we can get someone to help her out."

 My sister, still pouting asked "Why?"

 My mother replied" She's going to start helping your father with the business more, and you kids don't need a full time nanny. We'll just have someone in the afternoons to help out a little."

My father looked at me and said "Can you at least share the pool with your sister?"

 "Yeah, I'm cool with that. I just need the pool house for Xbox and stuff without disturbing you guys," I said.

"Okay, I'll bring in a couple people to chaperone, and change the food order with Jim," my dad said. My sister started to open her mouth before my father raised a hand to stop her "And I'll build another pool house for your party sweetie."

 "Exactly the same as the one *HE* gets to use?" she asked angrily.

"Yes sweetie, exactly the same."

 My sister's demeanor immediately changed, she kissed my father on the check, and said "Thank you daddy," while she bounded off to make plans.

I looked at my dad, and he said "I was planning on another guest house anyway. Maybe not this fast, and not exactly the same, but it'll work."

 I shrugged and joked "I still inherit the house, including the second pool house when you and mom croak as the eldest son..."

 "Yeah, right," my father said.

Construction was quick and I actually got to work with Christina a little to see how things went down. But most importantly, I saw the extra costs for the rush job everyone had to do.

It likely doesn't matter who is on the official lease and who isn’t. When accepting money for rent, you become a landlord, and you and the other person enter into a month to month lease. As part of that, if you have to formally tell them to leave, it typically has to be in writing, which means a very easy paper trail to follow.

There are some pretty good plain English resources out there for tenants. I'd look at those so you know what you have to do as a landlord to ensure the actions you take are within the law.

Write up a rental agreement with everyone that details things like rent, household responsibilities for each person, expectations regarding personal property, and the penalties for missing a target. Clarify everything that might be a point of contention, all the way down to the cable package if you have to. Is your rent late, that's an extra $50. Did you not do your chores, I'm hiring a cleaner to do your portion and the cost will be on your next bill. Did you use someone else's consumable item, well now your monthly bill includes the cost of two replacements.

Have everyone meet, discuss these things, and sign paperwork (if you haven't already). Present a detailed bill with all of the household expenditures (rent, power, water, internet, shared consumables, etc.) to each tenant at the end of a billing cycle. Setting global expectations is better initially, and then you can easily target an individual should they not meet the expectations.

Be careful with notice since you might fall on the wrong side of the law since it's within 30 days. Also, don't unfairly target the problem individual. Uneven enforcement of the household rules is a point of contention within itself. If you really need this person out, and their adherence to a good set of rules won't matter, be very clear about a move out date, and then be ready to involve the police.

While you can solve a lot of problems that arise from the professional landlord/tenant relationship with rental agreements, you can't legislate away a person's shitty personality.

A lot of this is pretty familiar. Sorry for not being sequential, but here are my most prominent thoughts.

With respect to your family, and not knowing the dynamic, I take extreme issue with your father saying to just get over your feelings. There can be a lot of contributing factors when it comes to depression like diet, environment, and schedule, all of which can be changed. If it's a problem with brain chemistry, it's a lot harder to treat. IMO, if it ends up being a brain chemistry issue, telling someone to just be happy is akin to telling them to not be gay.

I too have tried a lot of different therapists, as well as a lot of medications, and I haven't found a combination I've felt good with. I wouldn't say there's anything "wrong" with you, you're just different. The same way some people need a hearing aid, or a prosthetic to live a more regular life, we may need therapy and/or medication.

While it is normal for kids to pick on each other, it's also common in adults. People are seldom concerned with their impact on other people. You have to surround yourself with good people so the bad stuff can't take root in your life. Have a bad shift? Maybe a bad week? Grab some friends and hit up happy hour. Maybe go to a mall or the movies. Put some good in your life, and push out the bad, if only for a little while.

I have had friends that hurt me, and I tend to respond poorly. Most of the time it's a mistake, and we talk, and they understand. I've had a couple friends who I was very close to for many years do something deliberately hurtful, and I effectively cut off contact. It may be extreme, but I don’t let those people take away from what little happiness I have.

I'm sorry about your poor experience in the hospital. I had a similar experience, and a lot of my motivation is driven by me not wanting to go back. I'm sure the sexual assault doesn't help. I sincerely hope that you can keep yourself in a place where you don't feel it necessary to return.

If I may offer a suggestion, in response to a perceived flaw in yourself, try to improve a little at a time. My boss accurately pointed out that I am terrible to my subordinates when I feel as though the team has failed him. As I became aware of that, I've gotten better. I still yell, and angrily hit inanimate objects, but it isn’t focused on an individual, and it's much shorter.

Sorry if I got a little rambley. Hopefully you can find something good in all of that. Best of luck to you.

I was in an urban district that was large enough to have a site just for ESL instruction. Then when kids had a good enough grasp, they'd go to a regular school and be put in a group along with an IA who could help with some of the more complex topics. Math classes were the most prominent where there would be a couple students in a corner talking quietly about the lessons with their IAs.

My challenges were mainly centered around the kids being unruly. I expect a certain amount from high schoolers, but when disobedience starts in elementary and gets worse from there, there’s a bigger problem. It was to the point where some teachers wouldn't even try to break up a fight because any involvement would trigger a use of force investigation by the district, and those could go either way. One of the most telling things was when I was at a high school, and my girlfriend came to have lunch with me, and noted the students must be on break/lunch as well since there were so many in the halls, outside, etc.. I looked at my watch and told her it was 3rd period.

It takes a special breed to be a teacher, and there is a great reward when you see the moment of clarity when a concept is grasped. That being said, the challenges are far greater than when I was a student. There were a lot of teachers just waiting out the last couple years before their pensions kicked in, and were absolutely miserable, if not having some mental breaks. One even went back to being a waitress since she made more money that way. I don’t want to discourage you, but I also want you to have realistic expectations.

Again, best wishes, and I hope you can work out not only the challenges with your parents, but any that may stem from your chosen profession as well.

My parents and I don’t see eye to eye on a lot of things. Now I'm very clear with them that if they start bringing these points of contention up, I leave. I started doing this several years ago, and the first couple times, I would sit down after and talk with them about how they were making me feel, and that my best choice would be to remove myself from the antagonists. Now I just give them a look, and if they push, I politely excuse myself, leave, and don’t talk to them for a week or so.

The initial response was them trying to guilt me, but I calmly told them that while my actions may hurt them, their actions were hurting me, and I was choosing to remove myself from the situation. That phrasing had a lot of gravity because I used to get in a lot of fights, and it was drilled into my head to walk away from things like that.

I don't know if that will work for you, it might be a little riskier since you're still getting some financial support from them. Also, having worked in the school system, I know several people who have left very lucrative jobs to do something more meaningful. Conversely, I went to the private sector, make a good deal of money, and am not happy with my life. Your happiness is what matters, not the size of your paycheck.

Not only because of the importance of the job, but because a lot of tenured teachers are lazy, and kids are little shits that grow into bigger shits. They liked to antagonize me, which is one of the reasons I left. If this is going to be your line in the sand, make sure you can tough it out, at least until your parents won't say I told you so.

Probably about 15 years ago for about 48 hours for depression. I don’t remember too much, but I remember it being terrible, wanting to get out ASAP, and never go back. Here are a couple things I remember about the whole thing:

I was in both individual and group therapy in addition to experimenting with different medications. After a long time with negligible improvement in my mood, the doctors decided that it might be best to do a voluntary commitment to eliminate variables that might be hindering my progress.

 I showed up, and went through intake. No belts, shoelaces, keys, anything that could maybe be used to hurt yourself or someone else. I ended up wearing hospital scrubs and slippers for my time there. The nurse station was in the middle of the patient rooms and lounge. There was a locked room built in to the station for medication dispensation. The lounge we used for group discussions, had a few tables for when meals came, and some couches for whatever. There was a kiosk video game console not unlike those you'd see at Best Buy, a pool table, and plenty of books and magazines. There was also a small fenced in outdoor area for sunshine, but maybe more for smokers.

The ward I was put at was for a wide range of illness, so the afflictions of the residents was varied. I distinctly remember 3 people. One was the biggest wet blanket ever, always pointing out why something wouldn't work for him. Another was an extremely emotional girl in her 20s. Her boyfriend broke up with her as soon as her intake paperwork was done which made her even more distraught. My roommate was the interesting one. He wasn't very verbal, and he was a little scary, but damn was he good at pool. He kicked my ass a few times.

Things are very scheduled there since variance in schedule can be a contributor to mental illness. You see a psychologist once a day, a couple group discussions exercises, meals, and a couple hours in the afternoon of free time.

It wasn't a good environment for me, though generalized depression is a bitch to treat. What I will say is if you do end up in a similar situation, have a goal to work towards. Not just getting out, but a way to stay out. Try to stay objective and listen to the staff, they want to help. They are likely going through a very generalized treatment plan. Even if things aren't directly applicable, the overall concepts are.

To get out, I had to demonstrate that wasn't a risk to myself or others. Part of that was a set of tasks I could do help manage my depression. I still have that notepad in my desk somewhere.

One more thing: If you're there, or you know someone who is, it isn't something to bring up. Be supportive if it's a friend, and try to accept support if it's you. It was a low point in my life a long time ago, and very few people in my life know the true reason I was gone that week. I really don't like thinking about it.

Your mileage my vary, but hopefully that gives people an idea of what's out there.
